lead: This unit explains how spark-ignition and compression-ignition engines receive fuel, and how spark-ignition engines make and time the spark. It moves from carburettor mixture demand to mechanical and electronic injection, nozzles and spray, governors, and battery/magneto ignition. After it you can size simple fuel flows, read injection layouts, choose pump and nozzle types, and set spark advance.
about: Chapter 2.1 sets the SI mixture target and shows why a carburettor needs several circuits. 2.2 classifies injection systems and states their requirements; 2.3 details jerk pumps, distributor pumps and unit injectors; 2.4 moves to common rail, where pressure and timing are separated. 2.5 covers electronic mono-point, multi-point and gasoline direct injection. 2.6 follows the fuel through the nozzle into spray, penetration and atomisation. 2.7 explains governors that hold diesel speed by moving the fuel rack. 2.8 compares battery-coil and magneto ignition, and 2.9, taught by only a few universities, covers spark advance and timing. Each chapter uses the earlier one: mixture demand sets metering, pumps create pressure, injectors create spray, and ignition hardware needs timing control.

chapters.idea: A carburettor must vary the air-fuel ratio with load and speed, and separate circuits do that for idle, cruise, power and acceleration.
chapters.depth: Cover the SI engine mixture demand first: air-fuel ratio (A/F) by mass, chemically correct petrol about 14.7:1, rich idle about 12:1, cruise 15–16:1, full load about 12.5:1, and extra fuel for acceleration. Explain venturi depression, float chamber, main metering jet, idle circuit, power/economy valve, accelerator pump and choke. Some syllabi call the circuits idle, main, power, accelerator and choke. Show why one fixed jet cannot meet all loads.

figure.title: Mixture target against load
figure.aria: A line graph of required air-fuel ratio against engine load, starting rich at idle, leaning at cruise, and becoming rich again at full load.

chapters.example: An engine takes 0.045 kg/s of air. The carburettor is set for 15:1 by mass. Petrol density is 750 kg/m³. Find fuel mass flow and volume flow. Fuel mass flow = 0.045/15 = 0.003 kg/s. Volume flow = 0.003/750 = 4×10⁻⁶ m³/s = 4 cm³/s.
chapters.trap: Thinking the main jet alone sets the mixture at all loads; acceleration and choke are extra-fuel circuits.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: SI engine four-stroke cycle and air-fuel mixture basics.
chapters.leave: Combustion stages, knock and flame speed to Unit 3; emission formation to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A fuel injection system must meter, atomise, distribute and time fuel; its types are classified by air assist, direct or indirect injection, and control.
chapters.depth: Cover requirements of a fuel injection system: accurate metering, atomisation, distribution to each cylinder, correct timing and pressure. Classify types: air injection (air-assisted, obsolete) and solid injection (airless); direct and indirect injection; mechanical and electronic; continuous and intermittent. Define injection timing as start of fuel delivery and injection lag as the delay from pump delivery to nozzle opening. Some syllabi call solid injection airless injection.

figure.aria: A classification tree of fuel injection systems, splitting into air injection and solid injection, then direct and indirect forms.

chapters.example: A four-cylinder four-stroke diesel engine uses 6 kg/h of fuel at 1800 rpm. Find the fuel delivered per injection per cylinder. 6 kg/h = 0.1 kg/min. Injections per cylinder per min = 1800/2 = 900. Total injections/min = 4×900 = 3600. Fuel per injection = 0.1/3600 = 2.78×10⁻⁵ kg = 27.8 mg.
chapters.trap: Confusing direct injection with direct control; forgetting four-stroke injection frequency is rpm/2 per cylinder.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: SI and CI working principles; chapter 2.1 for SI mixture.
chapters.leave: Pump construction to 2.3; rail hardware to 2.4; nozzle geometry to 2.6.

chapters.idea: Mechanical diesel pumps generate injection pressure by plunger motion and time delivery by spill or distribution; unit injectors combine pump and nozzle at the cylinder.
chapters.depth: Cover the jerk (in-line) pump: cam, plunger, barrel, helix, spill port, delivery valve and effective stroke; fuel quantity set by rotating the plunger. Cover the distributor pump: one plunger, rotor and cam ring feeding each cylinder in turn. Cover the unit injector: cam-driven pump and nozzle in one unit at the cylinder, with no long high-pressure pipe. Compare applications, timing marks and limitations. Some syllabi call the jerk pump a plunger pump or in-line pump.

figure.title: Jerk pump delivery
figure.aria: A block flow of a jerk pump: cam lift moves the plunger, the spill port closes, pressure opens the delivery valve, and the nozzle injects.

chapters.example: A jerk pump plunger has diameter 8 mm and effective stroke 3 mm. Find fuel delivered per injection. Area = π(0.008²)/4 = 5.027×10⁻⁵ m². Volume = 5.027×10⁻⁵×0.003 = 1.508×10⁻⁷ m³ = 150.8 mm³.
chapters.trap: Taking total plunger stroke as effective stroke; the spill port closes only after the inlet port is covered.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.2 injection types; Unit 1 four-stroke timing.
chapters.leave: Common rail pressure control to 2.4; nozzle spray to 2.6; governor speed control to 2.7.

chapters.idea: Common rail stores fuel at high pressure in one rail and uses ECU-controlled injectors, so pressure and injection timing can be set independently.
chapters.depth: Cover the common rail layout: tank, lift pump, filter, high-pressure pump, rail, pressure sensor, pressure control valve, electronic control unit (ECU) and solenoid or piezo injectors. Rail pressure is typically 1000–2000 bar. Explain independent control of pressure and injection timing, pilot/main/post injection (split and multiple injection), and benefits: better atomisation, lower noise and lower emissions. Mention cost and complexity as limits. Some syllabi call this common rail diesel injection.

figure.title: Common rail layout
figure.aria: A common-rail layout: fuel runs from tank through lift pump and filter to a high-pressure pump, then to a rail and injectors, with the ECU controlling rail pressure and injector timing.

chapters.example: An injector delivers 30 mm³ per injection. The engine is a four-cylinder four-stroke running at 3000 rpm. Find fuel flow in L/h. Injections per cylinder per min = 3000/2 = 1500. Total injections/min = 4×1500 = 6000. Volume/min = 30×6000 = 180000 mm³/min = 180 cm³/min = 0.18 L/min = 10.8 L/h.
chapters.trap: Saying rail pressure sets injection quantity alone; quantity depends on rail pressure and injector open time together.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.2 types; chapter 2.3 mechanical pump limits.
chapters.leave: Detailed nozzle spray to 2.6; ECU sensor details to 2.5.

chapters.idea: Electronic fuel injection uses sensors, an ECU and solenoid or piezo injectors to meter fuel; mono-point injects at the throttle body, multi-point at each port, and GDI injects directly into the cylinder.
chapters.depth: Cover electronic fuel injection (EFI) parts: sensors for air flow or manifold pressure, throttle position, coolant, oxygen and crank position; ECU; fuel pump; pressure regulator; injectors. Explain open loop and closed loop with the oxygen sensor. Compare mono-point (single-point or throttle-body injection, one injector) with multi-point (port injection, one injector per cylinder) and sequential/batch firing. Cover gasoline direct injection (GDI): fuel injected directly into the cylinder at high pressure, with homogeneous or stratified charge. Some syllabi call mono-point single-point injection.

figure.title: Electronic fuel injection loop
figure.aria: A closed-loop electronic fuel injection block diagram: sensors send signals to the ECU, which pulses injectors into the engine, and the O2 sensor feeds exhaust information back to the ECU.

chapters.example: An injector flows 240 cm³/min when fully open. It is held open for 5 ms. Find fuel delivered per injection. 240 cm³/min = 4 cm³/s. Volume = 4×0.005 = 0.02 cm³ = 20 mm³.
chapters.trap: Mixing up mono-point and multi-point locations; thinking GDI is the same as port injection.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.2 injection types; chapter 2.4 common rail for the high-pressure direct injection idea.
chapters.leave: Spray atomisation to 2.6; spark timing to 2.9; emission control to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The nozzle turns fuel pressure into a spray; hole size, hole number, opening pressure and injection pressure set atomisation, penetration and cone angle.
chapters.depth: Cover nozzle types: pintle, single-hole, multi-hole and throttle nozzles; opening pressure and sac volume. Cover nozzle tests: pop tester for opening pressure and spray pattern, and leak test. Explain spray formation: atomisation, droplet size (Sauter mean diameter, SMD), cone angle, penetration and mixing with air. Show how injection pressure, hole size, hole number and air density change the spray. Some syllabi call multi-hole nozzles multi-orifice nozzles. Keep split and multiple injection in 2.4.

figure.title: Nozzle spray chain
figure.aria: A block flow from high fuel pressure through a five-hole nozzle, where the jet breaks into droplets, penetrates the chamber and mixes with air.

chapters.example: A nozzle has 5 holes, each of diameter 0.25 mm. Find total flow area. Area per hole = π(0.00025²)/4 = 4.909×10⁻⁸ m². Total area = 5×4.909×10⁻⁸ = 2.454×10⁻⁷ m² = 0.245 mm².
chapters.trap: Using nozzle hole diameter instead of radius in the area formula; assuming more holes are always better without matching penetration and air motion.
chapters.leave: Air motion and combustion chamber geometry to Unit 3; injection pump timing to 2.3.

chapters.idea: A governor holds engine speed by sensing speed and moving the fuel rack; mechanical centrifugal and pneumatic types are the common exam forms.
chapters.depth: Cover the need for a governor on diesel engines: no throttle, so speed must be held by varying fuel. Explain mechanical centrifugal governor: flyballs, sleeve, spring, lever and fuel rack (the control rod that sets pump delivery). Explain pneumatic governor: butterfly valve, vacuum and diaphragm. Cover droop, isochronous operation and stability. Mention hydraulic and electronic governors briefly. Some syllabi call the centrifugal type a mechanical governor.

figure.title: Governor speed control loop
figure.aria: A governor control loop: set speed is compared by the governor, which moves the fuel rack, changing engine fuel and actual speed, which feeds back to the governor.

chapters.example: A centrifugal governor has a ball of mass 0.1 kg at radius 50 mm rotating at 1200 rpm. Find the centrifugal force on one ball. ω = 2π×1200/60 = 125.7 rad/s. F = mω²r = 0.1×125.7²×0.05 = 79.0 N.
chapters.trap: Thinking the governor sets fuel quantity directly; it sets speed by changing fuel, while quantity still depends on load.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.3 pump fuel rack; Unit 1 engine speed and load.
chapters.leave: Electronic engine management to 2.5 and 2.9; emission effects to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Battery-coil ignition takes energy from the battery and magneto ignition makes its own; both use an induction coil to produce the spark.
chapters.depth: Cover battery-coil ignition: battery, ignition switch, primary winding, contact breaker, condenser, secondary winding, distributor and spark plugs. Explain how breaking primary current induces high secondary voltage. Cover magneto ignition: rotating magnet or armature, primary coil, contact breaker, condenser and distributor; it makes its own current and needs no battery. Compare both for cost, starting, speed and maintenance. Mention electronic ignition as a contact-breaker replacement. Some syllabi call battery-coil ignition coil ignition.

figure.title: Battery-coil ignition
figure.aria: A battery-coil ignition block diagram: battery current through the switch builds in the primary coil, the contact breaker interrupts it, the secondary coil sends high voltage to the distributor and spark plug.

chapters.example: A coil has primary inductance L = 6 mH and current I = 4 A at the instant the contact breaker opens. Find the stored energy. E = ½LI² = 0.5×0.006×16 = 0.048 J = 48 mJ.
chapters.trap: Saying a magneto needs a battery; confusing primary current with spark current.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 SI engine cycle; chapter 2.5 electronic control basics.
chapters.leave: Spark advance and knock to 2.9 and Unit 3; distributor advance mechanisms to 2.9.

chapters.idea: Spark timing must move earlier as speed rises and load falls, so spark advance is scheduled to get peak pressure near TDC without knock.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter. Cover spark timing relative to top dead centre (TDC), spark advance (also called ignition advance), centrifugal advance with speed, vacuum advance with load, timing light check and knock-sensor retard. Use the sample schedule 1000 rpm: 10°, 2000 rpm: 20°, 3000 rpm: 30°, 4000 rpm: 40°. Explain too-advanced spark (knock) and too-retarded spark (lost power, overheating). Keep it shorter than the other chapters.

figure.title: Spark advance against speed
figure.aria: A line graph of spark advance against engine speed, rising from ten degrees at one thousand rpm to forty degrees at four thousand rpm.

chapters.example: At 1000 rpm the spark advance is 10°; at 3000 rpm it is 30°. Find the advance at 2500 rpm if the schedule is linear. Slope = (30° − 10°)/(3000 − 1000) = 20°/2000 rpm = 0.01°/rpm. Advance = 10° + (2500 − 1000)×0.01 = 25°.
chapters.trap: Thinking advance is fixed; high load needs retard to avoid knock, while high speed needs more advance.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.8 ignition systems; Unit 3 knock and combustion.
chapters.leave: Knock chemistry to Unit 3; emission effects to Unit 6.
